query: Why do handling times differ by channel and priority?

per_column.name: issue_type
per_column.rationale: Provides a genuine new categorical axis to group handling times, well beyond the coarse original 'priority'/'channel'. All sampled values (billing_dispute, auth_or_access_failure, service_outage, feature_request, data_problem) are sound readings of the source text. Strong grounding and high analytical leverage for explaining why handling times vary.

per_column.name: customer_impairment_scope
per_column.rationale: Scope/blast-radius is a strong explanatory dimension for handling-time differences, distinct from priority. Samples are well grounded: enterprise production downtime, single_user session issue, single_tenant_single_feature for the invoice/CSV cases, not_present for the pure feature request. Categorisations are warranted inferences from the text.

per_column.name: resolution_intervention
per_column.rationale: The type of remediation is a useful axis to explain handling-time variation. However, this column asserts resolution actions the source text does not state. For CS-0001 (invoice correction) it produces 'bug_fix_or_hotfix' and for CS-0002 (session drop suspected SSO config) also 'bug_fix_or_hotfix' where the issue descriptions describe the problem, not the resolution taken. These are confident specifics unsupported by the request text, indicating some fabrication despite plausible category vocabulary.

judge.rationale: All three added columns supply genuine, non-redundant categorical axes (issue nature, blast radius, remediation type) that directly help explain why handling times differ beyond the existing priority/channel fields. issue_type and customer_impairment_scope are both useful and well grounded in the source text. resolution_intervention is analytically valuable but its values describe actions/outcomes that the issue_description (a request/report) frequently does not state, leading to unsupported confident assertions in at least two of five sampled rows, which lowers overall groundedness.
